title: Little faith (Matthew 14:22–36)
hookLine: fine until you look at your feet: Peter on the water, warning or model?
tomorrow: can your hands be spotless while your heart isn't?

lines: IT IS I; BE NOT AFRAID.
cards: First time on a paddleboard, or on skates: you're steady until you look down at your feet. Then the wobble starts. Peter does exactly that, on water.
It's night, the boat is tossed with waves, and a figure comes toward them walking on the sea. They cry out that it's a spirit. Then the voice: "Be of good cheer; it is I; be not afraid."
Peter answers: "Lord, if it be thou, bid me come unto thee on the water." One word comes back: "Come."

teach.b: And Peter climbs out and walks.

Then: "But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me. And immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and said unto him, O thou of little faith, wherefore didst thou doubt?"
Christians read Peter here in two ways.

teach.h: A WARNING: EYES OFF HIM, SINKING.
teach.b: Some hear a warning. Peter had the word come, and he took his eyes off the one who said it. The question, wherefore didst thou doubt, is a real rebuke, and the point is plain: keep looking at him, not at the wind.

teach.h: A MODEL: THE ONE WHO STEPPED OUT.
teach.b: Others hear a model. The others stayed in the boat; one climbed out. He walked before he sank.
When he went under, his prayer was three words long, and it worked.

teach.h: THE HAND FIRST, THE QUESTION AFTER.
teach.b: And look at the order: the hand comes first, immediately, and the question comes after, with Peter already held. On this reading, little faith is still faith, enough to get out of the boat.
Both readings quote the same verses, and Matthew gives both a place. Then the wind stops, and those in the boat worship him: "Of a truth thou art the Son of God."

how: Some Christians pray Peter's three words, Lord, save me, in moments of fear, and some churches tell the story to children as a picture of keeping your eyes on Jesus.

o: small, wavering faith that's still faith
faith held by only a few in the crowd

games.q: on the water — tap the pairs.
p: it is I; be not afraid
he was afraid, and began to sink

s: Peter sank the moment he stepped out of the boat
he walked on the water first; he began to sink when he saw the wind boisterous.
Jesus asked why Peter doubted before he caught him
immediately Jesus stretched forth his hand, and caught him, and then asked.
afterward, those in the boat worshipped him
"Of a truth thou art the Son of God."

games.q: a friend says: Peter is a cautionary tale, he doubted and sank. make the best case for the other reading.
o: Peter never really sank; the story is only a metaphor.
he alone stepped out, and the hand came first; little faith is still faith.
Jesus praised Peter's doubt as a kind of wisdom.
games.why: the model reading quotes the text: Peter walked, cried Lord, save me, and immediately Jesus caught him before asking. the warning reading quotes the same verse: wherefore didst thou doubt?

practice: If you can, stand, fix your eyes on one point ahead of you, and take one slow step toward it. Feel the floor take your weight. Then stay there, still, and breathe, the way someone stands just after a step they weren't sure of.

wordCard.voice: Little faith. What Jesus calls Peter's faith on the water: small, wavering, and still enough to climb out of the boat.

orig.note: Greek for O thou of little faith: one word in Matthew 14:31, little-faithed.

carryVoice: Your line: reach out your hand. In Matthew, the hand comes before the question. Be well.
